clue.text: The red stone is all in order, Sir

definitions.meaning: a deep red gem, commonly set in jewellery
Victorian slang naming General Wolseley, 'all Sir' plus his forename, meant everything shipshape

explanation.surface: A jeweller assures a customer that the ruby-coloured stone is in perfect condition.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped 'is all in'; the page prints them. 'All Sir Garnet' was a British catchphrase of the 1870s and later, after the famously efficient commander Wolseley, for 'everything correct'.
explanation.definitionFit: This gem is classically red, and the general's name became shorthand for perfect order, so both halves point to one word.

clue.text: Granddad in jug?

definitions.meaning: an old man, pictured with a whiskery grey chin
a stoneware drinking jug with a bearded face moulded on it, also called a bellarmine

explanation.surface: Grandfather is in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jug' looks like slang for prison but is the bearded stoneware jug; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An elderly man and a big glazed jug decorated with a bearded mask both have this name.

clue.text: Miss Stone, not easy to read

definitions.text: Miss Stone, not easy to read

parts.words: Miss Stone, not easy to read
parts.note: a lady surnamed Stone with a forename, which together name the inscribed slab that unlocked hieroglyphs

explanation.surface: A woman named Miss Stone has illegible handwriting or an inscrutable manner.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous stone in the British Museum carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, so it was hard to read until deciphered.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename that, joined to Stone, names the trilingual slab found in Egypt in 1799.

clue.text: Big buyers find it absorbing

parts.note: absorbing in the sense of interesting, but also the old trade practice of buying up the whole supply to corner a market

explanation.surface: Shopping on a large scale holds the attention of major purchasers.
explanation.walkthrough: Historically, to engross was to buy up stock wholesale so as to control prices, which is what big buyers do.
explanation.definitionFit: It means gripping the attention, and in old commerce it was buying up goods in bulk to corner the market.

clue.text: In fine mine's worried-she's bound to be

indicators.note: worried means shaken up, so the letters of fine and mine are jumbled together

parts.note: taken as written
the word mine, its 's giving no letter

explanation.surface: Someone fretting about a fine at the mine, with an aside about a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges FINE plus MINE into the answer; 'In' is a link. The definition says a woman is certain to have this quality.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman is bound to be womanly in grammar and nature, the quality of the female sex.

clue.text: Not that the manicurist need be one politically

definitions.text: Not that the manicurist need be one politically

parts.words: Not that the manicurist need be one politically
parts.note: a manicurist works on the extremities, the fingertips, so is literally a worker on extremes

explanation.surface: A remark that a nail technician need not hold radical political views.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'extrem-ist', the word suggests someone who tends extremities like fingers, which a manicurist does without any politics.
explanation.definitionFit: A person holding radical political views is called this, and the word also suggests a carer for extremities.

clue.text: Rum-ti-Foo was a balmy one

parts.note: W. S. Gilbert's Bab Ballad The Bishop of Rum-ti-Foo is set on a warm South Sea island

explanation.surface: Describing an imaginary place with a nonsense name as mild and pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balmy' hints at 'barmy' (British for mad), but means warm and mild, as Gilbert's tropical island is.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert's Rum-ti-Foo is a small island, and a small island is called by this word.

clue.text: The possibility of re-doing the whole thing is disregarded

indicators.note: re-doing the whole thing means every letter of the word re-doing is set out again in a fresh order

parts.note: the letters of re-doing, without the hyphen

explanation.surface: A suggestion to start the entire job over again is brushed aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging all of RE-DOING gives the answer; 'The possibility of' and 'is' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something paid no attention is overlooked or disregarded.

clue.text: What the oil did to the locks didn't call for an antimacassar!

definitions.text: What the oil did to the locks didn't call for an antimacassar!

parts.words: What the oil did to the locks didn't call for an antimacassar!
parts.note: oil on door locks loosens them, while Macassar oil on hair locks needed a cloth on the chair back

explanation.surface: Hair oil on someone's locks without the protective chair cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Locks are both door mechanisms and hair. An antimacassar is the cloth on a chair back that kept Macassar hair oil off the upholstery; oil on a door lock merely frees it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lubricating oil makes a stiff lock move more freely, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: William as he appeared in close-up eponymously

indicators.note: close-up taken as closed up: the two words as and he run together with no space

explanation.surface: An actor named William, filmed in close-up, playing a role named after himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close-up' means the words AS HE closed up into one. 'eponymously' points to Mrs Humphry Ward's novel The Marriage of William Ashe, named for its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The title hero of a Victorian novel has William as his first name and this as his surname.

clue.text: Flags of the ancients

definitions.meaning: banners or standards flown by ships and regiments
'ancient' is an archaic word for a standard-bearer, as Iago is Othello's ancient

explanation.definitionFit: These are banners, and the old title 'ancient' for a standard-bearer is the same rank as this officer.

clue.text: Gifts of money?

parts.note: gifts read as natural abilities, while the ancient Greek weight of silver was a unit of currency

explanation.definitionFit: The word means natural aptitudes and was also a large sum of money in the ancient world, as in the parable.

clue.text: With which to get the measure of De Profundis?

definitions.text: With which to get the measure of De Profundis?

parts.words: With which to get the measure of De Profundis?
parts.note: De Profundis is Latin for 'out of the depths', so the clue asks for an instrument that gauges sea depth

explanation.surface: Asking what yardstick could judge Oscar Wilde's prison letter.
explanation.walkthrough: De Profundis is the title of Oscar Wilde's letter from Reading Gaol and of Psalm 130; taken literally it means 'from the depths'.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrument for sounding the deep sea, so it literally takes the measure of the depths.

clue.text: You can't hit this nail on the head!

definitions.text: You can't hit this nail on the head!

parts.words: You can't hit this nail on the head!
parts.note: the idiom 'hit the nail on the head' meets a slim nail made with little or no head

explanation.surface: A remark that someone has missed the point entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the idiom for getting something exactly right; literally, this small wire nail has almost no head to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A slender, nearly headless wire nail used for flooring and fine joinery.

clue.text: Above the west, mountainous clouds: it beats everything

parts.note: above means over
a helm, or helm cloud, is a cap of cloud sitting on a mountain top, as on Cross Fell in Cumbria

explanation.surface: A weather report: huge clouds piled over the western sky, outdoing all else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mountainous' suggests huge, but means clouds that sit on mountains. 'the' and 'it' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat everything is to swamp or overpower it completely.

clue.text: Gathered in the same sad haphazard way'

indicators.note: arranged in a haphazard way means the letters of same and sad are put in random order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy crowd assembled in the usual sorry, disorganised fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a haphazard way' scrambles SAME and SAD; 'in the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather a fortune or a crowd is to accumulate it, piled together.

clue.text: It sets off with a bang

definitions.text: It sets off with a bang

parts.words: It sets off with a bang
parts.note: sets off read as starts out lively, but meaning a device that triggers an explosive

explanation.surface: Someone or something starting a journey or event in grand style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sets off with a bang' is the idiom for a lively start, literally a device that fires an explosive charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuse or cap that triggers an explosive charge is literally what sets off the bang.

clue.text: Red Ivan? Nobody asked him to come

definitions.text: Red Ivan? Nobody asked him to come

parts.words: Red Ivan? Nobody asked him to come
parts.note: a Soviet soldier, a Red named Ivan, arriving uninvited across a border

explanation.surface: A Soviet soldier turns up unwelcome, a Cold War worry.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue pictures an uninvited Russian soldier; the letters of 'Red Ivan' also rearrange to the answer, but no clue word signals that, so the picture carries it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who crosses a border uninvited and by force is an aggressor entering another's land.

clue.text: About those 4 relatives, they're in the opposition

parts.note: re is a Latin-derived word for about, concerning, as in business letters
4 points to the answer at 4 across, which means female, so female relatives

explanation.surface: Gossip about four family members who are against something.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' is not a number but a cross-reference to 4 across: relatives of that kind are women.
explanation.definitionFit: People who oppose or withstand something are fighting against it, like a wartime resistance.

clue.text: Like the subject of Ravel's pavane

definitions.text: Like the subject of Ravel's pavane

parts.words: Like the subject of Ravel's pavane
parts.note: Ravel's piece is Pavane pour une infante défunte, a pavane for a dead princess

explanation.surface: A music-lover describes the person the famous Ravel dance was written about.
explanation.walkthrough: The French title of Ravel's Pavane for a Dead Princess contains the answer's French form, so the subject is dead.
explanation.definitionFit: The princess of the title is no longer living, and the word means dead or extinct.

clue.text: Like the flatterer's treatment of mules

indicators.note: the treatment given to the words of mules is a reworking of their letters

parts.note: the letters of of and mules

explanation.surface: Comparing the way a sycophant handles stubborn mules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treatment' rearranges OF MULES; 'of' is fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive, cloying praise is what a flatterer heaps on, so it describes the flatterer's manner.

clue.text: Jack reaches his objectives

parts.note: a jack tar, or jack, is an old name for a sailor, shortened to tar
to reach a place is to get there

explanation.surface: A man called Jack achieves the goals he set himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' reads as a man's name but is the sailor, TAR; 'his' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aims and goals are things aimed at, like the rings on an archery butt.

clue.text: Being a small enclosure in existence

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation sits inside the Latin word

parts.note: esse is Latin for to be, used in English for existence, as in 'in esse'
small means shortened: enc is the abbreviation for enclosure on a letter

explanation.surface: Life described as a tiny pen within the wider world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small' signals the abbreviation ENC, which goes inside ESSE. 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing's fundamental nature, its very being, is what makes it what it is.

clue.text: Horse-pistol

definitions.meaning: a revolver made by Samuel ... company

explanation.definitionFit: A young male horse and the brand of revolver from the American gunmaker share the name.

clue.text: How a horse-dealer manages ?

parts.note: an old name for a horse-dealer is a coper, so what a horse-dealer does is deal, and the verb also means gets by

explanation.surface: A question about how someone selling horses gets along.
explanation.walkthrough: In dialect English 'to cope' was to barter, especially horses, so the dealer literally does this.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means deals with things successfully, and once meant bartering horses.

clue.text: In contrast, rivalling the half-sister

parts.note: rivalling means being against, opposed, so anti
taken as written

indicators.note: half of the word sister means its first three of six letters are kept

explanation.surface: A family comparison: one woman competing with her half-sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-sister' looks like a relative but means half the word SISTER. 'In' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A direct opposite or sharp contrast is the meaning of this rhetorical term.

clue.text: Tommy's war programme

parts.note: Tommy Handley's BBC radio comedy, It's That Man Again, ran through the Second World War

explanation.surface: A British soldier's wartime plan of campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tommy' suggests a British soldier, but is the comedian Tommy Handley, whose BBC radio show was a wartime morale-booster known by its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The initials of It's That Man Again, Tommy Handley's hugely popular wartime radio comedy.

clue.text: Bobby was on it, Tom Piperson was it

definitions.meaning: a bobby, a British policeman, walks a regular patrol route
in the nursery rhyme Tom, Tom, the piper's son stole a pig, and 'Tom was' thrashed

explanation.definitionFit: A police officer's round and the past participle meaning thrashed, from the rhyme's line 'the pig was eat and Tom was ...'.

clue.text: What the planners throw out ?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'What the planners throw out ?' gives PROJECT (a plan; to throw out), not the filed PROTECT; no parse gives PROTECT and the crossing letter cannot be checked here.

clue.text: What a mix-up, when you see me embracing a fallen angel!

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the word me wraps round the rest

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a fallen angel has tumbled from grace, so the letters of angel tumble into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the confusion of seeing oneself hugging a disgraced angel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fallen' suggests a sinful angel but signals an anagram; 'embracing' makes ME the outer piece. 'when you see' and 'a' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A medley or jumble of things is what this borrowed French word means.

clue.text: Loud speakers in classical design

parts.note: loudspeakers read as people with booming voices, named after a herald in Homer's Iliad

explanation.surface: Audio equipment made in a classical-style cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: Stentor was the Greek herald in the Iliad whose voice was as loud as fifty men's, so the classical figure gives a word for very loud talkers.
explanation.definitionFit: People with very powerful voices are called after Homer's loud-voiced herald.

clue.text: You've got Jenny to reckon with !

definitions.meaning: a jenny is a female donkey, playfully read as a female ass, ass plus the feminine ending -ess
to reckon here is to estimate or evaluate

explanation.surface: A warning that a formidable woman called Jenny will have to be dealt with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jenny' looks like a woman's name; it is a she-donkey, and a female ass would be an ass-ess, the answer's spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A female donkey treated as a feminine noun, and the verb to evaluate or judge, share one spelling.
